prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Now that I have your face by heart, I look Less at its features than its darkening frame Where quince and melon, yellow as young flame, Lie with quilled dahlias and the shepherd’s crook. Beyond, a garden. There, in insolent ease The lead and marble figures watch the show Of yet another summer loath to go Although the scythes hang in the apple trees. Now that I have your face by heart, I look. Now that I have your voice by heart, I read In the black chords upon a dulling page Music that is not meant for music’s cage, Whose emblems mix with words that shake and bleed. The staves are shuttled over with a stark Unprinted silence. In a double dream I must spell out the storm, the running stream. The beat’s too swift. The notes shift in the dark. Now that I have your voice by heart, I read. Now that I have your heart by heart, I see The wharves with their great ships and architraves; The rigging and the cargo and the slaves On a strange beach under a broken sky. O not departure, but a voyage done! The bales stand on the stone; the anchor weeps Its red rust downward, and the long vine creeps Beside the salt herb, in the lengthening sun. Now that I have your heart by heart, I see.

outputs.L2:
Since I know your face from memory, I no longer study the separate parts of it so much as the shadowed border around it, where quinces and melons, yellow like new fire, rest beside quilled dahlias and a shepherd’s crook.

Farther back is a garden. There, with arrogant stillness, figures made of lead and marble observe the spectacle of one more summer reluctant to end, though scythes are already hanging in the apple trees.

Since I know your face from memory, I look.

Since I know your voice from memory, I turn to the dark chords on a fading page and read a music that cannot be confined inside music’s formal bars, whose signs mingle with words that tremble and seem to bleed.

Across the staves moves a harsh, unwritten quiet. In a doubled dream, I have to decipher the storm and the flowing stream. The rhythm races too quickly; the notes alter in the darkness.

Since I know your voice from memory, I read.

Since I know your heart from memory, I perceive the docks, the huge ships, and the architraves; the ropes, the freight, and the enslaved people on an unfamiliar shore beneath a fractured sky.

Not a leaving, but a journey already completed. The bundles sit on the stone; the anchor sheds red rust like tears, and the long vine stretches near the salt plant in the growing sunlight.

Since I know your heart from memory, I see.
outputs.L3:
The poem portrays love as an act of deep memorization and inward transformation. The speaker has studied the beloved’s face so intensely that it no longer appears only as a physical presence. Instead, it begins to emerge through the surrounding world: in the shapes and colors of fruit, in flowers, in garden statues, and in the atmosphere of a fading summer. These images suggest that the beloved has become inseparable from the speaker’s perception. The face is not merely remembered; it is projected onto the landscape, appearing everywhere the speaker looks.

This connection between memory and the visible world also links beauty to the passage of time. The seasonal imagery, especially the sense of summer nearing its end, gives the poem an elegiac quality. Beauty is present, but it is also fragile and temporary. The speaker’s memory becomes a way of preserving what time threatens to change or take away. As the season fades, the beloved’s image remains vivid within the speaker’s mind, suggesting that memory can hold beauty even as the external world moves toward decline.

The poem also explores the internalization of the beloved’s voice. The speaker has absorbed it so completely that written music is transformed into something unstable, silent, and emotionally charged. Music, which should normally provide sound and structure, becomes uncertain and inward. The beloved’s voice no longer exists simply as something heard; it becomes a powerful inner presence. This transformation gives the poem a sense of emotional intensity, as though the memory of the voice is more haunting than the voice itself.

Through these images, the poem presents love as a form of profound knowing. The speaker’s love moves beyond ordinary recognition of physical features or sound. The beloved is no longer understood only through face and voice, but through symbolic landscapes and objects that carry emotional meaning. Fruit, flowers, statues, music, ships, and rust all become part of the speaker’s attempt to grasp the beloved more fully. Love, in this sense, is not just attachment or desire; it is an imaginative act that reshapes the world.

In the final section, the poem turns inward even further by imagining the beloved’s heart. Rather than using conventional images of romance, it describes the heart through ships, cargo, rust, and the idea of a completed voyage. These images suggest weight, history, distance, and endurance. The heart is not pictured as beginning a journey, but as having already traveled, carried its burdens, and arrived somewhere. This emphasis on completion rather than departure gives the ending a reflective, mature tone. Love is presented not as a fresh adventure, but as something marked by experience, memory, and the traces left behind by time.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores the power of intimate memory to transform perception. Its repeated claim that the speaker knows the beloved’s face, voice, and heart “by heart” suggests more than simple familiarity. To know someone “by heart” is to have internalized them so completely that they become part of one’s own consciousness. The beloved is no longer merely an external presence to be observed, heard, or touched; instead, the beloved becomes a way through which the speaker experiences the world.

This idea develops through a series of richly symbolic images. The poem moves through scenes associated with art, music, and voyage, each of which becomes a metaphor for love remembered and reimagined. The beloved’s face may be read like a painting, the beloved’s voice recalled like music, and the beloved’s presence followed like a journey across distance. These images suggest that memory is not passive. It does not simply preserve what has disappeared; it actively reshapes the speaker’s surroundings, allowing ordinary perception to become charged with emotional meaning.

The phrase “by heart” is especially important because it links memory, love, and interpretation. It implies both memorization and affection: the speaker knows the beloved not only intellectually but emotionally and spiritually. This deep knowledge allows the speaker to “read” the world differently. Art becomes more vivid, music more resonant, and travel more meaningful because each experience is touched by the remembered presence of the beloved. In this way, the poem presents love as a kind of inner language, one that teaches the speaker how to see and understand more deeply.

The poem is significant because it refuses to treat absence as simple loss. Even if the beloved is distant, unreachable, or no longer physically present, the speaker’s repeated insistence on knowing them “by heart” turns absence into a form of possession. This possession is not controlling or material; it is imaginative and emotional. The beloved continues to exist within the speaker’s memory, shaping thought, perception, and feeling. The poem therefore suggests that love, once fully internalized, does not end with separation. Instead, it becomes an enduring presence, a source of vision, and a deeper way of reading the world.
outputs.L5:
**Now, Less, Where**

Now is the only place we truly have. It is the moment between what has already happened and what has not yet arrived. Yet we often miss it because we are busy wanting more—more time, more things, more answers.

But sometimes, less is what we need. Less noise, less worry, less pressure to be everywhere at once. With less in our hands and minds, we can finally notice what is around us: the quiet room, the open sky, the people nearby, the breath we are taking.

And then comes the question: where? Where are we going? Where do we belong? Where can we find peace?

Maybe the answer is not far away. Maybe it is here, now, in a life made lighter by choosing less.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a formal ekphrastic love poem beginning “Now that I have your face by heart,” with rich Renaissance still-life imagery, repeating refrains, and three stanzas focused on face, voice, and heart.
counterfactuals.output:
Now that I have your face by heart, I keep  
its light as painters keep a bowl of pears—  
gold leaf beside the citron’s dimpled sleep,  
a silver knife, a quince, a spray of hairs  
of saffron loosening from a painted saint.  
Your brow: the marble ledge where lilies lean;  
your eyes: two plums, dark-glazed, without complaint;  
your mouth: a pomegranate split between  
its ruby vows. I look, and looking learn  
how beauty ripens under time and art.  
Still, where the candles flower, shadows burn:  
**I praise what I remember and what I cannot part.**  

Now that I have your voice by heart, I hear  
its amber pouring through the room like wine,  
a viol’s honeyed gut-string, low and clear,  
the psalm of bees around a muscat vine.  
It lifts the linen napkin, stirs the rose,  
sets figs to blush beside the pewter plate;  
it rings in crystal where the lamplight glows  
and makes the painted oyster articulate.  
If silence falls, it falls as velvet falls  
over a chalice—dark, but not apart;  
within that hush your hidden music calls:  
**I praise what I remember and what I cannot part.**  

Now that I have your heart by heart, I hold  
no relic richer in a chapel’s gloom:  
a peach bruised softly into dusk and gold,  
a clove-stuck orange breathing through the room,  
a globe, a skull, a clock with gilded wing,  
all saying love is mortal, love is more.  
Your heart, my still life, keeps its living spring  
beneath the varnish time lays thinly o’er.  
Let empires tarnish, let the roses start  
their red surrender petal after petal;  
my hand returns to what it knows by heart:  
**I praise what I remember and what I cannot part.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a rhymed poem in the style of mid-20th-century formalist poetry about memorizing a beloved so deeply that paintings, sheet music, and seascapes become metaphors for love and loss.
counterfactuals.output:
I learned you as a painter learns the grain  
Of linen, where the undercolors start;  
As rain remembers roofs, as roofs retain  
The silver, slanting signature of rain—  
So I rehearsed the weather of your heart.

I knew the small allegro of your hand,  
The margin where your laughter would begin,  
The rests your silence placed in every band  
Of speech, like notes no instrument had planned  
Yet all the listening room was gathered in.

Now every canvas takes your absent light:  
A bowl of pears grows tender with your name;  
A hillside, bruised with evening, turns outright  
Into the blue you wore that April night—  
And loss steps forward, framed in gilt and flame.

I read the staves where old sonatas sleep;  
Their black notes climb like birds across the snow.  
The treble breaks; the buried cellos keep  
A vow too deep for melody to weep,  
And all the bars remember what I know.

The sea, meanwhile, repeats its learned refrain,  
Erasing what it writes along the shore:  
Foam like torn letters; gulls like notes of pain;  
The horizon drawn, then darkened, then drawn again—  
A door that opens only to restore

The room where you were living in my mind,  
Each look arranged, each word exact and near.  
Yet memory, that meticulous design,  
Makes masterpieces only to remind  
The hand it loves what it must lose to hear.

So let the painted fruit grow dim with dust,  
The music close, the tide withdraw its art.  
What I have memorized is more than trust:  
A shape the world assumes because it must—  
Your absence, learned by heart, become my heart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical poem with the repeated lines “Now that I have your face by heart,” “Now that I have your voice by heart,” and “Now that I have your heart by heart,” using elevated diction and iambic rhythms.
counterfactuals.output:
Now that I have your face by heart,  
I read the dawn in silver flame;  
The dark withdraws its ancient art,  
And every star forsakes its name.  

Your brow becomes the morning’s page,  
Your eyes, twin wells where heavens start;  
I turn from time, from grief, from age—  
Now that I have your face by heart.  

Now that I have your voice by heart,  
The winds take counsel from your breath;  
Their harps awake in field and mart,  
And summon lilies out of death.  

No bell can toll, no river plead,  
No bird ascend, no rain depart,  
But all the world repeats your creed—  
Now that I have your voice by heart.  

Now that I have your heart by heart,  
I bear its lamp through mortal shade;  
Its pulse has taught my own to start  
Where fear once knelt and sorrow prayed.  

O tender fire, O sovereign spark,  
O hidden sun, O sacred chart—  
I walk unlost through any dark,  
Now that I have your heart by heart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a dense, elegant poem about portraiture, music notation, and maritime imagery, where the speaker reflects on knowing someone “by heart”?
counterfactuals.output:
I know you by heart—  
not as the mirror knows its silver weather,  
nor as the painter, rinsing dusk from a brush,  
finds in the cheekbone a coast of returning light,

but as a score knows silence:  
those black birds moored on five fine wires,  
their wings instructing the hand when to tremble,  
when to rest.

Your face arrives in measures—  
brow, clef; mouth, a red diminuendo;  
the eyes, twin harbors dark with anchored stars.  
I have crossed them often, under weather,  
with only breath for sail,

and every likeness fails  
except the one the body keeps:  
salt in the pulse,  
a mast of bone,  
the heart’s small lantern swinging in its cage,

beating your name  
against the night’s notation.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a poem that sounds like an old formal English lyric: three stanzas, intricate rhyme, autumnal garden imagery, dark musical imagery, and a final voyage/harbor scene.
counterfactuals.output:
In gardens where the last pale roses lean,  
And yews make dusk before the dusk be due,  
The wet leaves whisper, gold and ashen-green,  
Of summers slain beneath a colder blue;  
There, where the fountain’s broken silver sighs,  
A blackbird drops one note, then lets it die—  
As though some viol, hidden from the skies,  
Had drawn a wound of music up on high.  

The orchards burn with lamps of tarnished flame,  
The spider strings his harp from thorn to thorn;  
Through every bough a minor wind makes claim,  
And shakes the pears like bells in cloisters worn.  
O sweet decay, O ceremonial grief,  
What anthem moves beneath thy russet pall?  
The moon, a wafer, whitens leaf by leaf,  
While night’s deep organ gathers over all.  

Then let us pass, when all the paths are drowned  
In mist, and every gate is pearled with rime,  
Down to the quay where solemn tides resound,  
And lanterns rock like stars withdrawn from time.  
There waits the bark, her sable canvas furled,  
Her prow toward seas no morning shall restore;  
Yet far beyond the margins of the world  
Some harbor rings with music evermore.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
